# The benchmarking problem in quantum optimization

## A field defined by fragile advantage claims

Few areas of computational physics have produced as many advantage claims, and
as many retractions of those claims, as quantum optimization. The pattern is by
now a genre: a quantum or quantum-annealing platform demonstrates a result on a
carefully chosen instance family, an advantage over classical methods is
asserted, and within months an improved classical algorithm matches or surpasses
the quantum runtime on the same instances. The lesson is not that quantum
hardware is uninteresting --- it is that *the benchmark, not the device, is
usually what is being tested*.

The most instructive recent episode concerns quantum simulation of spin-glass
dynamics. In 2023, a superconducting annealer was used to realize quantum
critical dynamics on thousands of qubits, extracting Kibble--Zurek critical
exponents that distinguished coherent quantum evolution from the slower
stochastic dynamics of analogous Monte Carlo algorithms [@king2023]. In 2025
this line culminated in a *Science* paper claiming beyond-classical computation:
simulating programmable spin-glass quench dynamics on lattices and evolution
times argued to be out of reach for state-of-the-art classical methods
[@king2025beyond]. Within the same month, two independent classical efforts
challenged the frontier. One used time-dependent variational Monte Carlo with a
Jastrow--Feenberg ansatz to reproduce the annealing dynamics at sizes previously
thought intractable [@mauron2025]; the other used two- and three-dimensional
tensor networks contracted with belief propagation to match the quantum
accuracies on hundreds of qubits with modest resources, ultimately appearing in
*Science* in 2026 [@tindall2026]. The quantum result was not "wrong"; rather, the
classical baseline against which it was measured moved.

This is the central epistemic difficulty. A quantum advantage is a statement
about *two* moving objects --- the quantum algorithm and the best classical
algorithm --- and the classical object is a research community, not a fixed
number. Any benchmark that does not anticipate classical improvement, and that
does not make the comparison reproducible and re-runnable as classical methods
evolve, will tend to certify advantages that do not survive contact with the
next preprint.

## Instance-family dependence: hardness is not generic

A second difficulty is that "hard optimization problem" is not a property of a
problem *class* but of an *instance distribution*. The same nominal problem ---
find the ground state of an Ising Hamiltonian on a given graph --- ranges from
trivially polynomial to NP-hard depending on the graph topology, the coupling
distribution, and whether a solution has been planted.

The canonical cautionary tale is the "glassy Chimera" analysis [@katzgraber2014].
Early D-Wave advantage studies used random instances on the hardware-native
Chimera graph. But Chimera is quasi-two-dimensional and of low treewidth, and
spin glasses on such graphs have a zero-temperature spin-glass transition and
narrow hardness window: their typical instances are *too easy* to expose any
quantum scaling advantage, because efficient classical methods (exact planar or
near-planar solvers, specialized cluster algorithms) dispatch them. The authors'
conclusion --- that better benchmarks must be *designed*, with hardness verified
rather than assumed --- remains the founding methodological principle for any
suite like BENQODHI, and was sharpened in the companion analysis of when spin
glasses can and cannot reveal speedup [@katzgraber2015].

The corollary is that benchmark *design* is a scientific activity in its own
right. One must choose instance families whose hardness is understood
analytically (so that one knows what is being tested), tunable (so that the
quantum--classical crossover can be located rather than guessed), and not
accidentally aligned with the inductive biases of any one solver.

## Unfair comparisons and the classical baseline

Even with well-chosen instances, comparisons are routinely unfair in ways that
inflate quantum performance. Common failure modes include: comparing optimized,
hardware-tuned quantum runs against single-core, untuned classical baselines;
omitting embedding and compilation overhead from the quantum time-to-solution;
reporting time-to-target on instances where the target is loose; and selecting
the favourable tail of an instance distribution.

The classical baseline question is the sharpest. Parallel tempering with
isoenergetic cluster moves (PT-ICM), population annealing, and the
specialized GPU implementations developed precisely *for* spin-glass ground-state
search are formidable; a fair benchmark must compare against these, not against
textbook simulated annealing [@kirkpatrick1983sa]. Recent work makes the stakes concrete.
Probabilistic computers (p-computers) co-designed with hardware to run
discrete-time simulated quantum annealing and adaptive parallel tempering were
shown to match or surpass the 2023 quantum-annealing spin-glass results, thereby
"raising the bar" for what a practical quantum advantage must clear
[@chowdhury2025] --- a result whose author list notably includes one of the
Sapienza groups central to BENQODHI. On the analog side, classical-mechanics
Ising machines based on simulated bifurcation achieve high-quality solutions at
remarkable speed [@goto2021sbm; @goto2019sbm]. And on the algorithmic-physics
side, a machine-learning-enhanced Monte Carlo scheme was shown, under controlled
and well-benchmarked conditions, to surpass simulated annealing and to be more
robust than population annealing on three-dimensional spin glasses
[@delbono2026]. Any suite that hopes to track progress toward quantum advantage
must therefore curate these classical and quantum-inspired baselines *as
first-class citizens*, not as strawmen.

## What "speedup" even means, and why standardization matters

The notion of quantum speedup is itself subtle. The influential analysis of how
to define and detect speedup distinguished provable, strong, potential, and
limited speedups, and showed that naive time-to-solution scaling can be
distorted by the choice of how many problems are solved, by suboptimal annealing
parameters, and by finite-size effects [@ronnow2014]. A benchmark suite that
does not commit to operational definitions --- which metric, at which target
quality, with which baseline, across which size range --- cannot adjudicate the
claims built on top of it.

The community has begun to respond with shared infrastructure. The Quantum
Optimization Benchmarking Library (QOBLIB), the "intractable decathlon," assembles
ten application-linked problem classes that are hard for classical solvers
already at modest sizes, with standardized instances and solution track records
[@koch2025qoblib]. This is an important step toward comparability and
reproducibility. As we argue in @sec-gap, however, QOBLIB's breadth (industrial
relevance across heterogeneous problem types) is complementary to, not a
substitute for, a *physics-grounded* suite organized around tunable disorder,
frustration, locality, and hardware-native topology --- which is precisely
BENQODHI's niche.


# Why spin glasses are the canonical hard benchmark

## Frustration and the structure of disorder

A spin glass is, in its simplest incarnation, a system of Ising variables
$s_i \in \{-1,+1\}$ with quenched random couplings,
$$
H(\mathbf{s}) \;=\; -\sum_{(i,j)\in E} J_{ij}\, s_i s_j \;-\; \sum_i h_i\, s_i ,
$$
where the $J_{ij}$ are drawn from a fixed distribution (e.g. $\pm 1$ with equal
probability, or Gaussian) on the edges of a graph $G=(V,E)$. The defining
feature is *frustration*: on any cycle whose product of coupling signs is
negative, no spin configuration can simultaneously satisfy all bonds. The
smallest example is a triangle with one antiferromagnetic and two ferromagnetic
bonds. Frustration is not a nuisance; it is the source of every interesting
property below.

The two archetypes anchor opposite ends of a connectivity axis. The
Sherrington--Kirkpatrick (SK) model places Gaussian couplings on the *complete*
graph, $J_{ij}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1/N)$ for all pairs [@sherrington1975]; it is the
mean-field paradigm, exactly solvable by the replica method but only after the
introduction of an infinite hierarchy of order parameters --- Parisi's replica
symmetry breaking (RSB) [@parisi1979; @parisi1980; @mezard1987]. The
Edwards--Anderson (EA) model places random couplings on a finite-dimensional
lattice (typically nearest-neighbour on a $d$-dimensional grid)
[@edwards1975]; it is the short-range paradigm, with local connectivity that
mirrors the locality constraints of physical hardware.

## Rugged landscapes, metastability, and broken ergodicity

Frustration plus disorder produces an energy landscape with an exponential
number of metastable states separated by barriers --- a "rugged" landscape. Two
qualitatively different kinds of barrier matter, and distinguishing them is
essential for interpreting any optimizer's behaviour:

- **Energetic barriers.** To pass from one low-lying configuration to another,
  the system must climb over high-energy intermediate configurations. Quantum
  tunnelling is conjectured to help precisely here, by passing *through* thin,
  tall barriers rather than over them.

- **Entropic barriers.** Even when no high-energy barrier separates good
  configurations, the *number* of paths leading toward a solution can be
  vanishingly small relative to the number leading away. Here the obstacle is
  the geometry of the solution set in configuration space, and tunnelling offers
  no obvious advantage. The 3-XORSAT analysis showed that on 3-regular random
  graphs the hardness is dominated by entropic barriers, which impede classical
  local algorithms and quantum annealing in similar ways [@bellitti2021]. A
  benchmark family that conflates these two mechanisms cannot diagnose *why* a
  given device succeeds or fails; a good suite must include instances that
  isolate each.

This landscape structure underlies *broken ergodicity*: below the spin-glass
transition temperature, the configuration space fractures into many pure states,
and physical or simulated dynamics can no longer explore it freely on accessible
timescales. The order parameter is not a magnetization but the *overlap
distribution* $P(q)$ between independent equilibrium configurations, whose
non-trivial (non-self-averaging, broadly supported) shape is the signature of
RSB.

## Phase transitions and tunable hardness

Spin glasses possess genuine thermodynamic phase transitions, and this is what
makes their hardness *principled* rather than anecdotal. Classically, the
spin-glass transition at $T_{\mathrm{SG}}$ separates a paramagnet from the glassy
phase. Quantum-mechanically, adding a transverse field $\Gamma\sum_i \sigma^x_i$
to the Ising Hamiltonian drives a zero-temperature *quantum* phase transition at
a critical field $\Gamma_c$, separating a quantum paramagnet (large $\Gamma$)
from the spin-glass phase (small $\Gamma$). A quantum annealer must traverse
exactly this transition as it ramps $\Gamma$ to zero.

The behaviour of the spectral gap at this transition is the linchpin of
adiabatic optimization, and recent large-scale simulation has refined the
picture in a way directly relevant to benchmark design. For the two-dimensional
Ising spin glass it was shown that the minimum gap can close *algebraically*
rather than exponentially when the symmetry of permitted excitations is
restricted --- a distinction with direct consequences for whether quantum
annealing can offer a polynomial speedup [@bernaschi2024]. The accompanying
high-performance simulation codes make these gap studies reproducible
[@bernaschi2024qisg]. The take-away for BENQODHI is that the *quantum* hardness
of an instance family is a quantitative, simulable property --- it can be
measured, tuned, and used to place instances along a controlled difficulty axis.

Hardness can be tuned by other levers as well. *Planted-solution* constructions
fix a known ground state, enabling exact success measurement at sizes where
brute force is impossible. The "equation planting" technique casts an
efficiently solvable linear system over $\mathrm{GF}(2)$ as an Ising cost
function that nonetheless exhibits NP-hard-like landscape features
[@hen2019]; the 3-regular 3-XORSAT planted benchmark produces a "golf-course"
landscape --- a flat plateau punctuated by a narrow deep well --- that is
notoriously hard for local search and serves as a stringent stress test of both
classical and quantum heuristics [@kowalsky2022].

## Relation to QUBO and combinatorial optimization

The reason spin glasses are not merely a physics curiosity is the exact
equivalence between Ising ground-state search and Quadratic Unconstrained Binary
Optimization (QUBO). With $x_i = (1-s_i)/2 \in \{0,1\}$, any Ising Hamiltonian
maps to a QUBO and vice versa, and a remarkable range of NP-hard problems ---
graph partitioning, max-cut, vertex cover, number partitioning, colouring, and
many scheduling and routing problems --- admit compact Ising formulations
[@lucas2014; @glover2019qubo]. Finding the ground state of a general Ising spin
glass is itself NP-hard [@barahona1982]. Consequently, a device or algorithm
that demonstrably accelerates spin-glass ground-state search on principled
instance families is, in a precise sense, accelerating a universal substrate for
combinatorial optimization --- which is exactly the value proposition BENQODHI
seeks to test.


# Why these benchmarks are diagnostic for quantum hardware

Spin glasses are not merely *hard*; their structure is specifically informative
about the failure modes of each major quantum optimization modality. We treat
the four modalities in turn.

## Quantum annealing

Quantum annealing (QA) interpolates from a transverse-field driver to the
problem Hamiltonian,
$$
H(t) \;=\; -A(t)\sum_i \sigma^x_i \;+\; B(t)\, H_{\mathrm{Ising}} ,
$$
ideally remaining in the instantaneous ground state [@kadowaki1998;
@santoro2002; @farhi2000adiabatic; @albash2018; @hauke2020]. The adiabatic
theorem ties the required
runtime to the inverse square of the minimum spectral gap $\Delta_{\min}$
encountered along the schedule. For hard spin glasses, $\Delta_{\min}$ can be
exponentially small in the system size, producing Landau--Zener diabatic
transitions out of the ground state. Whether the gap closes polynomially or
exponentially is therefore the single most consequential property of an instance
family for QA --- and, as noted, it is now a measurable quantity for
two-dimensional glasses [@bernaschi2024]; the broader theory of the quantum
adiabatic algorithm on random optimization problems, from the spin-glass
perspective, is reviewed comprehensively in [@bapst2013]. Spin glasses let one test the
*tunnelling* hypothesis directly, by constructing instances whose barriers are
predominantly energetic (favouring tunnelling) versus entropic (where tunnelling
should not help) [@bellitti2021].

Empirically, the QA story on spin glasses spans the full arc from foundational
demonstrations on fully connected instances [@venturelli2015] to recent,
genuinely large-scale results: scaling advantage in *approximate* optimization
using quantum annealing correction on high-precision 2D spin glasses relative to
PT-ICM [@munozbauza2025], and iterative cyclic annealing reaching deep low-energy
states on 5000-qubit instances [@zhang2024cyclic]. The persistent caveat ---
that hardware acceleration must be separated from a fundamental algorithmic
improvement, and that embedding overhead can dominate --- is exactly what a
disciplined benchmark must quantify.

## QAOA and gate-based variational algorithms

The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) prepares a variational
state by alternating $p$ layers of problem-Hamiltonian and mixer evolution
[@farhi2014qaoa]. Two structural facts make spin glasses ideal QAOA benchmarks.

First, *locality and depth*. Each problem layer entangles variables connected by
the interaction graph; for dense graphs (SK) this forces deep circuits, while for
sparse graphs the locality of low-depth QAOA limits how much of the graph any
qubit can "see." The constant-depth limitations of QAOA on large sparse
hypergraphs and spin-glass models are provable: at fixed $p$, the algorithm
cannot exploit global structure and its performance is bounded by local
considerations [@basso2022]. Conversely, in the mean-field SK limit, infinite-size
analysis yields concrete performance predictions [@farhi2022sk], recently
strengthened to numerical evidence that QAOA reaches a $(1-\epsilon)$
approximation of the SK optimum with depth scaling as $\mathcal{O}(n/\epsilon^{1.13})$
on average, via a spin-boson mapping simulated with matrix product states
[@boulebnane2025]. Spin glasses thus probe the *depth-versus-size* frontier that
defines QAOA's practicality.

Second, *encoding and parameter transfer*. Implementing all-to-all SK couplings on
a planar device requires either deep swap networks or an encoding. The
parity (LHZ) encoding trades qubit count for geometric locality; benchmarking it
on spin glasses revealed that, at fixed layer count, its energy advantage over
random guessing *vanishes* as $N^{-1/2}$ --- a sobering scaling result that only
a spin-glass stress test could expose [@wybo2024], and one produced by a team at
a neutral-vendor hardware company. On the hardware-native side, whole-chip QAOA
for higher-order Ising spin glasses on IBM heavy-hex graphs exhibits strong
parameter concentration, enabling transfer of optimized angles across sizes up to
127 qubits [@pelofske2024; @pelofske2024short; @pelofske2023qavqaoa], with the
limits of such transfer for geometrically local cubic terms now being mapped
[@pelofske2026transfer]. These are precisely the higher-order, hardware-compatible
spin-glass families BENQODHI must include.

## Analog and coherent Ising machines

Analog Ising machines --- coherent Ising machines, optical and electronic
oscillator networks, and simulated-bifurcation accelerators --- minimize an
Ising Hamiltonian by mapping it onto the steady state or bifurcation dynamics of
a physical or simulated continuous system [@mohseni2022]. Their natural benchmark
is, again, the spin glass, because the spin-glass energy landscape is the generic
hard case these machines are built to attack. Simulated-bifurcation machines in
particular report strong performance on dense Ising problems [@goto2021sbm;
@goto2019sbm], and entanglement-assisted variational schemes built on generalized
coherent states have been benchmarked directly on the three-dimensional EA model
[@fioroni2025]. For these platforms the relevant axes are connectivity (all-to-all
vs sparse), coupling precision (analog machines are sensitive to the dynamic range
of $J_{ij}$), and the presence of higher-order terms --- all of which BENQODHI
parameterizes explicitly.

## Gate-based devices: embedding, locality, and routing

Finally, generic gate-based processors face the *embedding* problem head-on.
A logical interaction graph must be mapped to the device's fixed coupler graph,
incurring qubit-overhead and swap-depth penalties that grow with the mismatch
between logical and physical connectivity. This is why hardware-native topologies
matter: an SK instance is cheap on a fully connected logical model but expensive
on a heavy-hex chip, while a heavy-hex-native spin glass is cheap there and
artificial elsewhere. A benchmark suite that ignores topology will systematically
mis-rank devices. Spin glasses defined *directly* on Chimera, Pegasus, Zephyr,
heavy-hex, and unit-disk graphs let one measure the intrinsic capability of each
architecture without conflating it with embedding overhead --- and let one
measure that overhead deliberately when comparing across topologies. The detailed
construction of these families is the subject of the companion document.


# Recent literature, organized by paradigm {#sec-lit}

This section surveys 2023--2026 work in which spin-glass and related families are
used to assess a quantum (or quantum-inspired) algorithm or device. We organize
by *algorithmic paradigm*, not by year, and for each entry note the benchmark
family, the platform tested, the key finding, and the relevance to BENQODHI.

## Quantum annealing and analog quantum simulation

**King et al. (2023), *Nature* [@king2023].** *Family:* programmable 3D
cubic-lattice spin glasses, up to ~5000 qubits. *Platform:* D-Wave superconducting
annealer. *Finding:* quantum-critical Kibble--Zurek dynamics agree with
Schrödinger evolution on small instances and yield critical exponents
distinguishing coherent QA from Monte Carlo dynamics, supporting a scaling
advantage in *dynamics*. *Relevance:* establishes the 3D EA family at scale as the
reference battleground; defines the very instances later contested classically.

**King et al. (2025), *Science* [@king2025beyond].** *Family:* programmable
spin-glass quench dynamics across square, cubic, and diamond lattices.
*Platform:* D-Wave Advantage2 prototype vs Frontier supercomputer. *Finding:*
claim of beyond-classical computation for simulating quantum spin-glass dynamics.
*Relevance:* the headline advantage claim that BENQODHI-style reproducible,
re-runnable benchmarking exists to adjudicate.

**Mauron & Carleo (2025) [@mauron2025] and Tindall et al. (2026), *Science*
[@tindall2026].** *Family:* the same 2D/3D spin-glass annealing dynamics.
*Platform:* classical --- time-dependent variational Monte Carlo and 2D/3D tensor
networks with belief propagation. *Finding:* classical methods match the quantum
accuracies at hundreds of qubits with modest resources, narrowing or contesting
the frontier. *Relevance:* the decisive demonstration that classical baselines
move; any advantage metric must be designed to be re-evaluated as they do.

**Munoz-Bauza & Lidar (2025), *PRL* [@munozbauza2025].** *Family:* 2D spin glasses
with high-precision couplings. *Platform:* D-Wave Advantage with quantum
annealing correction. *Finding:* evidence for a QA *scaling advantage in
approximate optimization* relative to the strong PT-ICM baseline. *Relevance:*
shows that the right metric (approximate, not exact, optimization) and the right
baseline are essential design choices --- and that 2D high-precision glasses are
a productive family.

**Zhang, Boothby & Kamenev (2024), *Sci. Rep.* [@zhang2024cyclic].** *Family:*
5000-qubit spin glasses. *Platform:* D-Wave, iterative cyclic annealing.
*Finding:* deep low-energy states reached in record time; power-law cluster
structure in the low-energy landscape. *Relevance:* motivates landscape-structure
metadata (cluster-size distributions) as part of the benchmark protocol.

**Lopez-Bezanilla et al. (2025) [@lopezbezanilla2025].** *Family:* frustrated
Ising models on fullerene (geometric, low-degree) graphs. *Platform:* D-Wave.
*Finding:* programmable quantum dynamics on a non-lattice frustrated geometry.
*Relevance:* supports inclusion of geometric / non-standard low-degree graphs
beyond the usual lattices.

**Foundational anchors.** Theory of QA of an Ising spin glass [@santoro2002];
fully connected QA optimization [@venturelli2015]; coherent QA on a 2000-qubit
chain [@king2022coherent]; scaling vs path-integral Monte Carlo on frustrated
magnets [@king2021scaling]. These ground the modern results and supply the
methodological vocabulary (residual energy, time-to-solution, coherence).

## QAOA and gate-based variational optimization

**Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann & Zhou (2022), *Quantum* [@farhi2022sk].** *Family:*
SK at infinite size. *Finding:* closed-form QAOA performance in the
thermodynamic limit. *Relevance:* the analytic reference point for all SK--QAOA
benchmarking.

**Boulebnane et al. (2025) [@boulebnane2025].** *Family:* SK, infinite and
finite size up to 30 qubits. *Platform:* MPS simulation of a spin-boson mapping.
*Finding:* numerical evidence that QAOA approximates the SK ground state to
$(1-\epsilon)$ with depth $\mathcal{O}(n/\epsilon^{1.13})$ on average.
*Relevance:* sets a quantitative depth--quality expectation that hardware QAOA on
SK instances can be measured against.

**Basso, Gamarnik, Mei & Zhou (2022), FOCS [@basso2022].** *Family:* large sparse
hypergraphs and spin-glass models. *Finding:* provable limitations of
constant-level QAOA. *Relevance:* the theoretical reason sparse spin glasses are
indispensable --- they expose the locality bottleneck. (See also the high-depth
large-girth analysis [@basso2022highdepth].)

**Pelofske et al. (2024; 2023), *npj QI* / LNCS [@pelofske2024; @pelofske2024short;
@pelofske2023qavqaoa] and Pelofske et al. (2026), *PRR* [@pelofske2026transfer].**
*Family:* higher-order (cubic-term) random Ising spin glasses, heavy-hex-native,
16--127+ qubits. *Platform:* IBM superconducting processors; MPS for noise-free
reference. *Finding:* strong parameter concentration and transferable angles;
real hardware finds lower energies up to $p=2$--$3$; transfer limits mapped for
geometrically local cubic terms. *Relevance:* the template for the heavy-hex
higher-order family and for QA-vs-QAOA comparison on identical instances.

**Wybo & Leib (2024), *Quantum* [@wybo2024].** *Family:* SK spin glasses under
the parity (LHZ) encoding. *Finding:* fixed-layer energy advantage vanishes as
$N^{-1/2}$. *Relevance:* a clean demonstration that encodings must be benchmarked,
not assumed beneficial --- and that SK is the right stressor.

**Fioroni & Savona (2025), *Commun. Phys.* [@fioroni2025].** *Family:* 3D EA model.
*Platform:* entanglement-assisted variational ansatz (generalized coherent
states), thousands of spins. *Finding:* competitive solution quality and runtime
versus popular heuristics. *Relevance:* a quantum-inspired baseline benchmarked on
the EA family BENQODHI centres on.

## Neutral-atom and Rydberg optimization

**Ebadi et al. (2022), *Science* [@ebadi2022].** *Family:* maximum independent set
(MIS) on unit-disk graphs, up to 289 atoms. *Platform:* Rydberg atom arrays.
*Finding:* hardware-native encoding of UD-MIS via the Rydberg blockade.
*Relevance:* defines the geometric / unit-disk family for neutral-atom platforms.

**Nguyen et al. (2023), *PRX Quantum* [@nguyen2023].** *Family:* arbitrary-
connectivity problems mapped to weighted UD-MIS. *Finding:* explicit mappings with
at most quadratic qubit overhead. *Relevance:* clarifies how non-native problems
reach neutral-atom hardware, informing embedding-overhead metadata.

**Andrist et al. (2023), *PRR* [@andrist2023].** *Family:* UD-MIS, Union-Jack-like
connectivity. *Platform:* classical exact and heuristic solvers. *Finding:*
quasi-planar instances are solvable to optimality for thousands of nodes in
minutes; protocols proposed to *systematically tune* hardness. *Relevance:*
exactly the hardness-tuning philosophy BENQODHI adopts for the geometric family ---
and a warning that naive UD-MIS instances may be too easy.

## Probabilistic and physics-inspired classical baselines

**Chowdhury et al. (2025), *Nat. Commun.* [@chowdhury2025].** *Family:* 3D spin
glasses (the King-2023 instances). *Platform:* probabilistic computers running
DT-SQA and adaptive parallel tempering. *Finding:* match/surpass the quantum
annealer; establish a rigorous classical baseline. *Relevance:* a baseline
BENQODHI must include verbatim; co-authored by a core BENQODHI group.

**Goto et al. (2019; 2021), *Sci. Adv.* [@goto2019sbm; @goto2021sbm].** *Family:*
dense Ising / spin-glass problems. *Platform:* simulated-bifurcation machines.
*Finding:* high-quality solutions at high speed. *Relevance:* the analog/
quantum-inspired baseline for dense families.

**Del Bono, Ricci-Tersenghi & Zamponi (2026; 2025), *PNAS* / *PRE*
[@delbono2026; @delbono2025].** *Family:* 3D Ising spin glasses (QUBO).
*Platform:* machine-learning-enhanced global-annealing Monte Carlo. *Finding:*
demonstrable advantage over simulated annealing and greater robustness than
population annealing, under controlled benchmarking. *Relevance:* a state-of-the-art
ML-classical baseline, from a BENQODHI partner group, on the central family.

**Boettcher (2023) and Fan et al. (2023), *Nat. Commun.* [@boettcher2023;
@fan2023]; Ciarella et al. (2023), *MLST* [@ciarella2023].** *Family:* EA spin-glass
ground states; hard sampling problems. *Finding:* deep-reinforcement-learning
heuristics are competitive but their advantage is contested under fair
finite-size comparison; ML-assisted Monte Carlo can *fail* on genuinely hard
sampling. *Relevance:* a cautionary cluster --- ML baselines must be benchmarked
with the same rigour demanded of quantum ones; physics-inspired GNN approaches
[@schuetz2022gnn] and autoregressive neural samplers [@biazzo2024] belong in the
same comparison.

## XORSAT and higher-order benchmarks

**Hen (2019), *PRApplied* [@hen2019].** *Family:* equation-planted Ising instances
from linear systems over $\mathrm{GF}(2)$. *Finding:* a tool for benchmarking
Ising machines with known solutions and tunable structure. *Relevance:* the
methodological basis for planted-solution instances.

**Kowalsky, Albash, Hen & Lidar (2022), *QST* [@kowalsky2022].** *Family:*
3-regular 3-XORSAT with planted solutions and a "golf-course" landscape.
*Platform:* multiple classical and quantum heuristic optimizers. *Finding:* a
stringent, solution-known stress test that separates optimizers cleanly.
*Relevance:* the template for BENQODHI's 3-XORSAT family.

**Bellitti, Ricci-Tersenghi & Scardicchio (2021), *PRR* [@bellitti2021];
Bernaschi et al. (2021), *EPL* [@bernaschi2021xorsat].** *Family:* 3-regular
3-XORSAT. *Finding:* hardness dominated by *entropic* (not energetic) barriers,
affecting classical local search and quantum annealing alike; efficient GPU
algorithms set the classical bar. *Relevance:* explains *why* 3-XORSAT is hard
and what including it actually tests --- the barrier-type axis of the design
philosophy set out in the companion document.


# Why the literature still lacks a proper benchmark suite {#sec-gap}

The survey above contains excellent individual benchmarks. What it does not
contain is a *suite* with the four properties a community-scale comparison
requires simultaneously.

**1. Physics-principled hardness, not application-collected hardness.** QOBLIB
[@koch2025qoblib] is a landmark in standardization and reproducibility, but its
organizing principle is *practical relevance*: ten heterogeneous problem classes,
each hard at modest size, drawn from applications. That heterogeneity is a virtue
for industrial benchmarking and a limitation for *scientific* benchmarking, where
one wants to vary disorder, frustration, locality, and connectivity as
independent, controlled axes while holding the underlying physics fixed. BENQODHI
is deliberately narrower and deeper: a small number of spin-glass families
(SK, EA-2D/3D, sparse random-graph, 3-XORSAT) whose hardness is *understood
analytically* and can be *tuned continuously*, so that the quantum--classical
crossover can be located rather than merely observed.

**2. Hardware-topology awareness as a first-class axis.** Most existing
benchmarks are defined either on logical graphs (ignoring embedding) or on a
single vendor's native graph (ignoring portability). The glassy-Chimera lesson
[@katzgraber2014] showed that topology determines hardness; the heavy-hex QAOA
[@pelofske2024] and Rydberg UD-MIS [@ebadi2022; @andrist2023] literatures show
that each architecture has a *natural* family. A proper suite must include the
same physics expressed on Chimera, Pegasus, Zephyr, heavy-hex, and unit-disk
graphs, so that intrinsic device capability and embedding overhead can be
disentangled --- something no current single resource provides in one place.

**3. Reproducibility and re-runnability against moving classical baselines.** The
King-2025/Tindall-2026 episode [@king2025beyond; @tindall2026; @mauron2025] proves
that an advantage claim is only as durable as the protocol that lets it be
re-evaluated when classical methods improve. A suite must ship not just instances
but *baseline implementations* (PT-ICM, population annealing, simulated
bifurcation, p-computer DT-SQA/APT, ML-enhanced Monte Carlo) and a standardized,
versioned reporting format --- so that progress is *tracked*, not re-litigated.

**4. Diagnostic structure: separating mechanisms of hardness.** Energetic versus
entropic barriers [@bellitti2021], algebraic versus exponential gap closing
[@bernaschi2024], planted versus random instances [@hen2019; @kowalsky2022],
2-local versus higher-order interactions [@pelofske2024] --- these are the
mechanisms that determine whether a *quantum* device should be expected to help.
A suite organized around these mechanisms does more than rank solvers; it explains
*why* a solver wins or loses, which is what the field actually needs to make
progress.

BENQODHI's thesis is that filling this gap is not a matter of collecting more
instances but of *designing* a small, principled, topology-aware, baseline-bundled,
mechanism-diagnostic suite, maintained as living infrastructure. The companion
document, `benchmark_problem_families.qmd`, specifies the families, the proposed
hardware-native and geometric extensions, and the metadata and protocol that make
the comparison reproducible.
